# Exodus 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records three plagues — frogs (vv. 1–15), gnats/lice (vv. 16–19), and flies/swarms (vv. 20–32). Together they mark an escalation: the first two plagues (blood and frogs) struck from the Nile; these next three strike land and air. A critical shift occurs with the third plague — the magicians can no longer replicate the miracle and confess, "This is the finger of God." Another shift occurs with the fourth plague — Goshen is explicitly spared for the first time.

---

## Verses 1–4: Warning of the Second Plague — Frogs

**v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Go to Pharaoh and tell him that this is what the LORD says: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.'"**

The recurrent demand is repeated nine times across the plague narrative (Ex 5:1; 7:16; 8:1, 20, 21; 9:1, 13; 10:3, 4). God claims Israel as His own possession — not Pharaoh's. The demand is unconditional. The Septuagint uses the verb *latreuo* for "serve/worship," meaning to carry out religious duties in a spirit of worship.
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

The deliverance is not a release *from* all service but a change of masters — from serving Pharaoh to serving God, which is true freedom.
— Sermon Bible Commentary on StudyLight.org (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/exodus-8.html)

**v. 2 — "But if you refuse to let them go, I will plague your whole country with frogs."**

The Hebrew verb *nagaph* ("smite"/"plague") means to inflict a blow, usually from God and either fatal or disastrous. This same verb is used in Joshua 24:5 to summarize all ten plagues and in Exodus 12:27 for the Passover.
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

The frog was sacred in Egypt, associated with the goddess Heqet (or Heket), who was depicted with a frog's head and considered a goddess of fertility and procreative power. Egyptians could not intentionally kill frogs — doing so could be punished with death. God attacked Egypt with the very creature they worshipped.
— Ellicott's Commentary (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

Spurgeon observed: "There was a suitableness in God's choosing the frogs to humble Egypt's kings, because frogs were worshipped by that nation as emblems of the Deity… These be thy gods, O Egypt! Thou shalt have enough of them!"
— Precept Austin, quoting Spurgeon (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

**v. 3 — "The Nile will teem with frogs, and they will come into your palace and up to your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your officials and your people, and into your ovens and kneading bowls."**

The frogs' invasion of the most private and personal spaces — bedchambers, beds, ovens, kneading bowls — is supernaturally directed; frogs do not naturally behave this way. This is not some annual Nile phenomenon. Ellicott notes that Egyptians prized cleanliness above almost all nations; priests washed twice daily and twice nightly. Frogs in the bed and in the baking pans would have been an acute torment.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

Gill adds that the frogs would leap onto people's persons, into their laps and bosoms, making food nauseous and life intolerable.
— Gill's Exposition (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

The verb "swarm" (*sharats*) recalls Genesis 1:20 — the water would be swarming with frogs in abundance, an ironic reversal of creation.
— NET note, quoted at Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

**v. 4 — "The frogs will come up on you and your people and all your officials."**

Frogs literally upon Pharaoh himself — a direct, personal humiliation. The greatest monarch on earth, brought low by amphibians. Ryken quips, "By the time frogs started showing up under his bedcovers, even Pharaoh was starting to have his doubts about Heqet's power."
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

---

## Verses 5–7: The Plague of Frogs Executed

**v. 5 — "And the LORD said to Moses, 'Tell Aaron, Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers and canals and ponds…'"**

Aaron is the agent; Moses is the prophet. Matthew Henry says: "Aaron is ordered to draw out the forces, and with his outstretched arm and rod to give the signal of battle. Dictum factum — No sooner said than done."
— Precept Austin, quoting Matthew Henry (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

**v. 6 — "So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt."**

The Hebrew uses the singular "the frog" — designating the species collectively. The frogs "covered" the land.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 7 — "But the magicians did the same thing by their magic arts, and they also brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt."**

Though the magicians could duplicate the sign (likely through occult power, not mere trickery), all they accomplished was making the problem *worse*. They could not remove the frogs. Enduring Word notes: "For all their occult powers, all the magicians could do was make more frogs! They could only make the problem worse; yet their work gave Pharaoh an excuse to further harden his heart."
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

Ellicott takes a more skeptical view: the magicians only *seemed* to produce frogs through sleight-of-hand on a small scale, and "they would have shown their own power far more satisfactorily had they succeeded in taking the frogs away."
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

Gill says whatever they produced was done "by the help of devils" but "not in such numbers."
— Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

---

## Verses 8–15: Pharaoh Begs for Relief, Then Hardens His Heart

**v. 8 — "Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, 'Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people. Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.'"**

This is the first sign of yielding. Pharaoh had borne the water-to-blood plague without flinching — but the frogs struck *him personally*. Ellicott notes three concessions: (1) He acknowledged the power of Jehovah; (2) he acknowledged the power of righteous men's prayers; (3) he made an absolute, unreserved promise to "let the people go."
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

The NET note observes: "This is the first time in the conflict that Pharaoh even acknowledged that Yahweh existed."
— Precept Austin, quoting NET (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

Precept Austin adds: Pharaoh's request for prayer "was not a sign of Pharaoh's spirituality but only of his superstition. Many desperate people have called for a minister without ever really intending to call upon God."
— Precept Austin, quoting Ryken (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

Spurgeon noted: "There is a measure of faith which goes to increase a man's condemnation, since he ought to know that if what he believes is true, then the proper thing is to pray himself." Pharaoh asked for others' prayers but never prayed himself.
— Precept Austin, quoting Spurgeon (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

**v. 9 — "Moses said to Pharaoh, 'You may have the honor over me. When shall I pray for you… that the frogs… may be taken away…?'"**

"Glory over me" (KJV) or "You may have the honor over me" (BSB) is an unusual Hebrew phrase. Ellicott explains it as an Egyptian court courtesy meaning "I submit to thy will" or "I am content to do thy bidding." Moses gives Pharaoh the advantage of naming the time.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

Gill says Moses did this so that it would be clear the removal was not by chance or natural cause but by the Lord alone.
— Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 10 — "'Tomorrow,' Pharaoh answered. 'May it be as you say,' Moses replied, 'so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.'"**

Pharaoh's choice of "tomorrow" is puzzling given the distress. Gill suggests two reasons: (1) Pharaoh hoped the frogs might go away on their own by then; (2) he thought such a feat required elaborate rituals and time.
— Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

Moses' reply shows absolute confidence: the timing is set by Pharaoh, but the outcome will demonstrate that none compares to the Lord.
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

**vv. 11–13 — Moses prays; the frogs die.**

**v. 13** — "And the LORD did as Moses requested, and the frogs in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields died."

The frogs did not retreat to the river, nor were they eaten by birds. They simply died where they were. This was itself a miracle — frogs do not all die simultaneously across a whole nation.
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

**v. 14 — "They were piled into countless heaps, and there was a terrible stench in the land."**

Ellicott observes that God, knowing Pharaoh's insincerity, removed the plague in a manner that made its removal almost as bad as its continuance. The dead frogs piled up and rotted. He notes that in a historically recorded plague of frogs in Paeonia and Dardania (recounted by Eustathius), it was the stench that finally drove the people to abandon their country.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 15 — "When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, however, he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said."**

The Hebrew says there was "a breathing space" (*respite*). Pharaoh hardened his own heart. Ellicott notes that here Pharaoh's nature had finally been impressed (vv. 8–9); previously his heart was merely dull and callous. Now an impression had been made, and he had to call in his own will to efface it — this was the greater guilt.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

Enduring Word calls this the familiar pattern: "when relief comes, his heart returns to resistance, and each time he refuses God's call, the hardening deepens — just as gradual sin hardens the human heart." Spurgeon added: "Pharaoh increased his guilt. His vows heaped up his transgressions. He forgot his promises; but God did not."
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

---

## Verses 16–19: The Third Plague — Gnats (or Lice)

**v. 16 — "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Tell Aaron, Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, that it may turn into swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt.'"**

This plague came *without warning* — a judgment for Pharaoh's broken promise (v. 15). He was not given the option of avoiding it by submission.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

The identity of the "gnats" (*kinnim*) is disputed. The LXX and Vulgate translate it as "mosquitoes" or "gnats"; Josephus and Jewish commentators take it as "lice." Ellicott notes the word is likely onomatopoeic — from the sharp tingling sound of a mosquito on the wing. Most modern scholars favor gnats/mosquitoes.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

This plague struck at Egyptian religious practice: the Egyptian priesthood was obsessively clean, performing elaborate rituals of purification. An infestation of lice or gnats rendered them ceremonially unable to worship.
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**v. 17 — "…when Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, gnats came upon man and beast. All the dust of the earth turned into gnats throughout the land of Egypt."**

Gill notes the miraculous nature: lice do not normally spring from dust. This was like the creation of man from the dust — an act of almighty power.
— Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

The plague afflicted both man and beast, stopping the Egyptian sacrificial system — lice-infested animals could not be offered to the gods.
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**v. 18 — "The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not. And the gnats remained on man and beast."**

Here the magicians' power reaches its limit. Ellicott says gnats/mosquitoes were "things too delicate to be caught, and manipulated, and produced at a given moment by sleight-of-hand."
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

Enduring Word draws the theological point: "as great as Satan's power is, it is limited — and it comes to its limit rather early."
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**v. 19 — "'This is the finger of God,' the magicians said to Pharaoh. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said."**

The magicians confessed their impotence. Ellicott notes they said "finger of *a god*" (Elohim), not "finger of Jehovah." They acknowledged a supernatural power beyond their own but did not submit to the God of Israel.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

Precept Austin adds: "They did not use the name Jehovah but the name Elohim. One can only imagine Pharaoh's astonishment that his magicians were impotent regarding this miracle."
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

Pharaoh's heart was hardened even against the testimony of his own trusted advisers — an irrational resistance.
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

---

## Verses 20–24: The Fourth Plague — Flies (or Swarms)

**v. 20 — "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Get up early in the morning, and when Pharaoh goes out to the water, stand before him…'"**

As in Exodus 7:15, Pharaoh went out to the Nile in the morning — possibly for a religious observance. Ellicott conjectures this was during the great autumn festival when the first blades of corn appeared, and the god Khepra ("the creator") was especially worshipped.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 21 — "…I will send swarms of flies upon you and your officials and your people and your houses…"**

The Hebrew word *‘arob* is used in the singular and its exact meaning is uncertain. The LXX translates it "dog-fly" (*kynomyia*). Modern suggestions include a variety of insects, the *kakerlaque* (a biting beetle), or a mixed swarm. Psalm 78:45 indicates the swarm "devoured them," suggesting biting insects.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**v. 22 — "But on that day I will give special treatment to the land of Goshen, where My people live; no swarms of flies will be found there."**

This is the first explicit distinction made between Egyptians and Israelites in the plagues. Ellicott notes there was no natural barrier between Goshen and the rest of Egypt — the severance itself was a manifest miracle.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

Enduring Word: "This is the first mention of the idea that the land of Goshen… was spared in the plagues. Possibly, the people of Israel suffered at least somewhat under the previous plagues."
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**v. 23 — "I will make a distinction between My people and your people. This sign will take place tomorrow."**

God's purpose was that Pharaoh would "know that I, the LORD, am in the land" — not a distant deity but actively present and sovereign.
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

**v. 24 — "And the LORD did so. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh's palace… Throughout Egypt the land was ruined by swarms of flies."**

The Hebrew says the land was "corrupted" or "destroyed." Unlike previous plagues, this one damaged property — furniture, crops, everything. Ellicott says the *kakerlaque* "inflicts very painful bites" and damages materials, representing an advance in severity.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

---

## Verses 25–32: Pharaoh's Compromise and False Repentance

**v. 25 — "Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, 'Go, sacrifice to your God within this land.'"**

Pharaoh now tries negotiation. He "permits" worship but within Egypt's borders — a compromise. He still claims authority to dictate terms.
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

G. Campbell Morgan (quoted in Enduring Word): "That is the true attitude of the man of faith. Evil is always suggesting some compromise. To listen to it is to remain enslaved. The only way into liberty is to leave the land of evil."
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**v. 26 — "But Moses replied, 'It would not be right to do that, because the sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God would be detestable to the Egyptians… will they not stone us?'"**

Moses refused the compromise. The Hebrew sacrificial animals — sheep, goats, and cattle — were all sacred to Egyptians either nationally or in particular districts. Rams were sacred to Amun; cows to Isis; a bull-calf might be Apis. Sacrificing them before Egyptian eyes would be like "killing a pig in a Muslim mosque, or slaughtering a cow in a Hindu temple" (Cole, quoted in Enduring Word).
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

Ellicott adds that when a Roman ambassador accidentally killed a cat in Egypt, the populace tore him to pieces. Moses' fear was well-founded.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 27 — "We must make a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as He commands us."**

Moses held firm to the original demand (Ex 5:3). True obedience cannot be negotiated down to what feels safe or comfortable.
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**v. 28 — "Pharaoh answered, 'I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far. Now pray for me.'"**

Pharaoh concedes more — allowing departure — but adds "not very far," still trying to retain control. He also asks for prayer again ("Pray for me"), acknowledging dependence on Moses' intercession.
— Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 29 — "'…But Pharaoh must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go and sacrifice to the LORD.'"**

Moses rebukes Pharaoh openly. Ellicott notes: "God's servants must rebuke even kings when they openly break the moral law." Pharaoh had broken his unconditional promise from v. 8, and Moses was right to call it "deceit."
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 30 — "Then Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD."**

Moses intercedes just as he had promised. His faith in God's power did not eliminate the need for prayer — it drove him to it.
— Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 31 — "…He removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh and his officials and his people; not one fly remained."**

The total removal is as miraculous as the coming. Ellicott notes this sudden, complete removal is carefully recorded — "it seems not to have happened with the frogs or with the mosquitoes."
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

**v. 32 — "But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go."**

The pattern repeats: relief brings hardness. Pharaoh's heart is hardened "at this time also" — each cycle deepens the sclerosis. Enduring Word applies this to all people: "A man doesn't start by gambling away his paycheck; it starts with continuing on in friendly betting, and his heart grows hard… As we continue in sin and reject God's opportunities for us to repent and return, the hardening continues."
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Given the source limitations of this search, I can report only what surfaced from the approved sites:

**Reformed / Piper (Desiring God):** John Piper stresses that God "is a show-off" — He dragged out the ten plagues deliberately to display His power over gnats, frogs, flies, and everything. "God wants to be known as a very powerful God. And he wants to get glory over this rascal Pharaoh." This reflects a Reformed emphasis on God's sovereignty and self-glorification in judgment.
— Desiring God (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-living-god-is-a-missionary-god)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik affirms that the magicians' power was real occult/supernatural power, not mere illusion. "This wasn't the work of a skilled illusionist, this was occult power at work." He also notes the limit of Satan's power: "as great as Satan's power is, it is limited — and it comes to its limit rather early." This tradition tends to affirm the reality of spiritual warfare and demonic power while stressing God's superior authority.
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-8/)

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill, an older Baptist commentator, affirms the magicians' frogs were produced "by the help of devils," reflecting a traditional Baptist view of demonic involvement in counterfeit miracles. He also emphasizes that the Israelites may have been exempt from the frog plague itself (Gill cites R. Japhez on this).
— Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/8.htm)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott takes a more rationalist tone, suggesting the magicians used "sleight-of-hand" rather than genuine supernatural power. He also devotes considerable attention to Egyptian historical background and comparative ancient sources.
— Ellicott (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/8.htm)

**Methodist / Holiness:** No distinctively Methodist commentary on Exodus 8 emerged from Seedbed or Wesley sources in this search, though Matthew Henry (often used across traditions) emphasizes the universality of God's judgments and His sense of humor in using frogs: "God has many ways of disquieting those that live at ease."
— Precept Austin, quoting Matthew Henry (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

---

## Other Views

Because the search and fetch tools reached their limits, I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), or modern scholarly (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) content directly. However, the Precept Austin page did quote NET Bible notes at several points, indicating that modern evangelical scholarship affirms the supernatural character of the plagues against naturalistic explanations (e.g., the frogs did not merely emerge because the Nile was polluted — they appeared at Moses' command, covered all Egypt, and died simultaneously).
— Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-8-commentary)

No prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teachings on Exodus 8 surfaced in the searches of the approved sites.
